screens.title: Capstone: Build a Complete FPGA Embedded System
screens.narratorSegment: This capstone pulls together hardware design, embedded software, and verification into a single project you can demonstrate. You will design a digital oscilloscope and signal analyzer: sample an analog input with the MAX 10 ADC, store samples in on-chip BRAM as a circular buffer, apply a DSP block such as a 16-tap FIR or an FFT, and stream results to a PC terminal over UART. The NIOS II processor manages configuration, user controls, and UART traffic while custom Verilog handles the high-throughput ADC interface, buffering, and filtering. We will follow a disciplined flow: write a clear specification, build the Qsys system with IP and custom peripherals, implement and verify RTL in ModelSim, compile in Quartus Prime, then load and exercise the hardware with the JTAG debugger and logic analyzer. Along the way, you will make hardware-software partitioning choices and document testbenches, timing reports, and a demonstration video. By the end you will have a reproducible, graded project with clear deliverables. As you begin, think about which functions must run in hardware for performance and which are easier to manage in software—this is the core engineering trade-off you will practice.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Capstone Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Capstone: Build a Complete FPGA Embedded System

Design a digital oscilloscope: sample, buffer, filter, and stream. Combine NIOS II software with custom Verilog peripherals to demonstrate hardware-software co-design.

In this lesson
System spec, Qsys, Verilog, C, verification, demo.
Core focus
Hardware-software partitioning for real-time sampling.
Outcome
Working FPGA demo and a graded project report.
Explore Key Topics
System Spec
Define block diagrams, interfaces, and sample rates for a 1 MSPS ADC and 256-sample capture.
Qsys & IP
Integrate NIOS II, UART, ADC IP, timers, GPIO, and custom Avalon peripherals.
Verification
Use ModelSim testbenches, JTAG debugging, and logic analysis to prove behavior.
Visual Concept
NIOS II
Control, configuration, UART
Custom Verilog
ADC interface, circular buffer, FIR
Peripherals
UART, Timer, GPIO, BRAM
Deliverable
Working project, ModelSim testbenches, Quartus timing reports, demo video, and a written project report for grading.

screens.title: What you will be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this capstone you will be able to design a complete FPGA-based embedded system from a specification, integrate custom Verilog peripherals with a NIOS II soft-core inside Qsys, and write embedded C that runs on the processor to manage acquisition and communication. You will follow the FPGA design flow from Qsys assembly through Quartus Prime compilation, verify RTL in ModelSim, and program the hardware for live testing. You will test and debug with JTAG and logic analyzers, and produce a project report that documents block diagrams, RTL testbenches, timing results, and a demonstration video. Each objective maps to a concrete milestone: a working Qsys system, verified Verilog modules, a compiled bitstream, a running NIOS II application, and a recorded demo. These skills are essential because real embedded FPGA projects require coordination of hardware and software, clear verification evidence, and a reproducible delivery for grading or field use. Think about how each objective leads to a deliverable you can show — that clarity will help you plan and execute the project effectively.

screens.title: Define the system and requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Start by writing a concise specification that turns project goals into measurable requirements. For the recommended oscilloscope, specify the ADC channel, sampling resolution, required sample rate up to 1 MSPS, the capture window of 256 samples, buffer sizes, and the trigger mechanism that initiates a capture. Include precise interface definitions: UART baud (115200), button behavior (Button 1 toggles acquisition, Button 2 changes modes), LED status signals, and the NIOS II memories used for code and data. A clear spec avoids late rework: it tells you whether the FIR filter must be implemented in hardware for throughput or if a software routine on NIOS II is sufficient. Include performance constraints such as a 50 MHz system clock and timing margin for the ADC interface. As a concrete example, list the circular buffer as 256 samples in dual-port BRAM and the FIR filter as a 16-tap fixed-coefficient block. A common misconception is that vague goals are acceptable; in practice, missing or fuzzy constraints cause integration delays. Close with a checklist: block diagram, interface table, capture size, trigger conditions, and performance targets — these items become the foundation for Qsys and RTL work.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Project Specification
Definition

System Requirements

  • ADC: MAX 10, 12-bit, up to 1 MSPS.
  • Capture: trigger-based 256 samples, circular buffer in dual-port BRAM.
  • DSP: 16-tap FIR or FFT option.
  • Comms: UART at 115200 to PC terminal.
  • UI: Button 1 start/stop, Button 2 change filter/display.
  • Processor: NIOS II for control and UART handling.
Concrete Example
A clear spec entry:
Capture Window
256 samples at 500 kSPS, trigger when ADC crosses threshold, send captured block over UART as ASCII waveform or numeric values.
Why it matters
Concrete numbers let you choose BRAM size, CPU loop timing, and whether filtering must be hardware-accelerated to meet throughput.
Interface Table
List base addresses and data widths for ADC, UART, BRAM, GPIO.
Performance
Declare clock constraints (50 MHz) and acceptable latency for filter output.
Trigger
Define threshold crossing behavior, pre/post trigger samples, and capture confirmation via LED.

screens.title: Assemble the hardware system in Qsys
screens.narratorSegment: Qsys is where you assemble the system-level hardware: a NIOS II/f soft-core with its JTAG debug module, program and data memories, UART, timer, GPIO, and the ADC IP. You will add dual-port BRAM for the sample buffer and instantiate custom Avalon peripherals for the ADC interface and FIR filter. Assign base addresses carefully to avoid overlap and document them in your spec so your C code knows where to read and write. A concrete example from the chapter lists 64 KB on-chip memory for program and data, 8 KB of BRAM for the sample buffer, and a UART configured at 115200 baud connected to the USB-UART bridge. A common misconception is that adding IP is enough; in practice you must connect interrupt lines to the NIOS II, provide clocks and resets, and check bus width compatibility. After generating the Qsys system, export the top-level HDL and include the generated system in your top-level Verilog. Finish this step with a short sanity test: compile the board support package and run a trivial UART echo to confirm the communication path is functional. This early integration check saves time later when you add custom peripherals.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Qsys Architecture
Architecture
Core Qsys Components
  • NIOS II/f with JTAG debug module.
  • 64 KB on-chip memory for program/data.
  • 8 KB dual-port BRAM used as ADC sample buffer.
  • MAX 10 ADC IP core connected to analog input.
  • UART IP (115200) to USB-UART bridge.
  • Timer IP for periodic interrupts; GPIO for buttons and LEDs.
  • Custom FIR peripheral connected via Avalon bus.
Integration Tips
Assign non-overlapping base addresses, connect IRQ lines for timer and UART if used, and validate clock and reset routing. Export the BSP and test UART early.
Quick Test
After Qsys generation, build the BSP and run a simple UART echo or status print to confirm system connectivity before adding custom RTL.

screens.title: Design adc_interface and circular_buffer
screens.narratorSegment: Two custom Verilog modules are central to reliable acquisition: the adc_interface and the circular_buffer. The adc_interface reads the ADC IP core, detects valid samples, and presents a clean data-valid handshake to downstream logic. Define explicit signals: data_out, data_valid, write_enable, and a sampled timestamp or sample counter if needed. The circular_buffer implements 256-sample storage in dual-port BRAM. Use separate read and write pointers with modulo arithmetic for wrap-around and ensure that the write pointer advances only when data_valid is asserted. For dual-port BRAM, one port services writes from adc_interface while the other serves reads from NIOS II or the FIR filter. A concrete implementation detail: implement full/empty detection by tracking a sample count or comparing read and write pointers carefully. A common mistake is failing to handle concurrent read/write and reading stale data; mitigate this by using proper synchronizers when crossing clock domains or by using single-clock semantics if all logic shares the same clock. Close by writing a ModelSim testbench that drives ADC sample patterns and verifies buffer wrap-around and read-after-write correctness. Design adc_interface and circular_buffer means use dual-port bram with independent read/write pointers, clear data-valid handshake, and test wrap-around with a modelsim testbench.. In practical terms, signals, data-valid handshakes, dual-port bram access, and wrap-around logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › adc_interface & circular_buffer
adc_interface
Provide a stable data_valid signal and align sample timing to your system clock. Debounce or synchronize any asynchronous ADC-ready flags and tag each sample with a counter for trigger logic.
Signals
  • sample_out[11:0]
  • data_valid
  • write_enable
circular_buffer
Implement 256-depth dual-port BRAM with independent read/write pointers. Use modulo arithmetic and a sample count for full/empty detection.
Testbench idea
Drive a repeating ramp and random glitches from the ADC, assert trigger at threshold, and verify captured 256 samples and wrap-around behavior in ModelSim waveforms.
Common Mistake
Reading and writing pointers without synchronization across clock domains can produce corrupted reads. Either keep a single clock domain for ADC path or add synchronizers when crossing domains.

screens.title: Implementing a 16-tap FIR filter
screens.narratorSegment: A 16-tap FIR filter is a common choice for low-pass filtering of ADC samples. In hardware, implement it as a multiply-accumulate engine that reads a sample stream, multiplies by fixed coefficients, and accumulates results. Fixed coefficients let you use constant multipliers and possibly resource-saving optimizations. Pipeline the multiply-accumulate path to achieve higher throughput: break the operations into stages so each pipeline stage has less combinational delay, which raises the maximum clock frequency. The chapter recommends a hardware FIR to demonstrate hardware-software partitioning; use Avalon slave interfaces to feed samples from the circular buffer into the FIR peripheral and provide a ready/valid handshake for the filtered output. A concrete example: when the FIR is hardware-accelerated, the NIOS II can trigger the filter over a block of 256 samples and read filtered outputs at leisure over the bus. A common misconception is that more taps are always better; in practice, more taps increase latency and resource use. Close with a verification step: simulate the FIR input of a sine plus noise and confirm the expected attenuation or frequency response in ModelSim waveforms.

keyIdea.text: Pipeline the multiply-accumulate path and fix coefficients when possible to improve clock rate and resource efficiency.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › FIR Filter
Hardware FIR
Implement a 16-tap multiply-accumulate engine with fixed coefficients. Use shift-and-add or DSP blocks depending on available FPGA resources.
Pipeline
Break the MAC into stages to meet a 50 MHz constraint if needed. Pipelining increases throughput but adds latency.
Integration
Provide an Avalon slave that accepts blocks of samples or a streaming interface with ready/valid semantics. The NIOS II triggers a block run and reads outputs afterward.
Example Use
Trigger capture → move 256 samples into FIR → read 256 filtered outputs → send results to PC via UART.

screens.title: NIOS II software: main loop, ISRs, and UART
screens.narratorSegment: The NIOS II software orchestrates acquisition and user interaction. Start by initializing UART, ADC, timer, and GPIO. The main loop waits for a button press, starts ADC acquisition, collects 256 samples into memory or triggers the FIR filter, reads back filtered values, and sends them to the PC via UART. Implement a timer ISR to blink a status LED periodically so you know the system is alive. Include a UART command handler to change filter modes or trigger thresholds from the PC. The chapter includes a concrete temperature-monitoring C example that demonstrates reading the ADC, checking a button, and printing results periodically; use that structure for the oscilloscope code. A common mistake in embedded code is polling without debouncing buttons or without considering ISR preemption; prefer edge detection for button presses and keep ISR code short. After writing the application, test it first on the instruction set simulator, then on hardware with JTAG debug. The final step is to send captured data as ASCII numbers or a simple ASCII waveform so the instructor can verify functionality from the terminal output.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › NIOS II Software
Code Walkthrough
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include "system.h"

int main(void) {
  // Initialize UART, ADC, timer, GPIO
  // Main loop: wait for button, start ADC, collect 256 samples,
  // trigger FIR, read filtered outputs, send to PC via UART
  return 0;
}
Use the BSP generated by the SBT and test the main loop first in the simulator before hardware bring-up.
Practical Tips
  • Keep ISRs short: toggle LED and set flags for main loop to handle heavy work.
  • Debounce buttons or detect edges to avoid multiple toggles.
  • Print compactly to UART to avoid saturating the link; send binary only if both sides agree.
Concrete Example
Adapt the temperature monitor example to read ADC samples into a buffer, then format and print 256 values to the PC terminal once triggered.

screens.title: From spec to demonstration
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a stepwise design process to keep the project manageable and verifiable. The chapter lays out nine steps: specification, hardware design in Qsys, RTL design and ModelSim verification, integration into a top-level Verilog, synthesis and place-and-route in Quartus Prime, software development with the BSP and simulator testing, hardware-software integration with JTAG programming, testing and debugging using logic analyzers and the terminal, and documentation including block diagrams and test results. For each step produce a clear deliverable: a spec document, Qsys system files, RTL and testbenches, a compiled bitstream with timing reports, C source and a runnable ELF, captured waveforms and logs from the terminal, and a final report and demo video. An example milestone is: after generating the Qsys system, run a small UART print before adding custom peripherals; after each RTL module is added, run its ModelSim testbench to catch functional bugs early. A common misconception is trying to code everything at once; instead, iterate—prove each block independently, then integrate. This stepwise cadence reduces integration rework and provides the evidence graders expect. From spec to demonstration means specification → qsys → rtl → integration → synthesis → software → integration → test/debug → documentation.. screens.title: Decide what runs in hardware vs. software
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing which functions to implement in hardware versus software is a central design decision. Implement high-throughput, deterministic tasks like ADC interfacing, buffering, and the FIR filter in hardware when timing or parallelism is required. Tasks like user menus, UART command parsing, and non-time-critical control are typically better in software on the NIOS II because they are easier to iterate and debug. Use a concrete example: if the system must sample at 500 kSPS and apply a 16-tap FIR per sample, the multiply-accumulate work may exceed the NIOS II throughput unless you batch process or use hardware acceleration. A common misconception is to assume software flexibility always wins; however, software running on a soft-core often cannot match the parallel throughput of dedicated hardware. Contrast the two strategies: hardware FIR gives low latency and consistent performance but increases RTL complexity and synthesis time; a software FIR simplifies code but may require careful scheduling and may drop samples under load. End with a question to guide partitioning: does the task need sample-rate determinism or can you tolerate software scheduling and occasional latency? Decide what runs in hardware vs. software means put deterministic, high-throughput functions in hardware; keep control, ui, and flexible features in software.. In practical terms, throughput, latency, complexity, and debugability trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: ModelSim testbenches and common RTL mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is non-negotiable: write ModelSim testbenches for each Verilog module and inspect waveforms to show expected behavior. For the adc_interface, simulate ADC sample bursts and validate data_valid timing. For the circular_buffer, simulate continuous writes and reads to ensure no data corruption at wrap-around. For the FIR, stimulate with a sine and confirm attenuation. The chapter also provides exam examples that highlight frequent mistakes: a combinational always block that omits an else branch creates a latch; a sequential always block using blocking assignments can lead to simulation/synthesis mismatches. For example, the multiplexer snippet that assigns y only when sel is true will infer a latch unless an else assigns the other input. The counter example uses blocking assignment in a clocked block; replace equals with non-blocking less-than-or-equals semantics to model registers correctly. Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Verification & Pitfalls
Example Bug: Latch Inference
module mystery (
  input wire [3:0] a, b,
  input wire sel,
  output reg [3:0] y
);
  always @(*) begin
    if (sel)
      y = a; // Missing else causes latch inference
  end
endmodule
Fix: add an else or default assignment to avoid unintended latches.
Example Bug: Blocking in Sequential
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst)
    count = 8'b0; // Use non-blocking <= for registers
  else
    count = count + 1;
end
Fix: use non-blocking assignments to model register updates correctly.

fullNarratorScript:
This capstone pulls together hardware design, embedded software, and verification into a single project you can demonstrate. You will design a digital oscilloscope and signal analyzer: sample an analog input with the MAX 10 ADC, store samples in on-chip BRAM as a circular buffer, apply a DSP block such as a 16-tap FIR or an FFT, and stream results to a PC terminal over UART. The NIOS II processor manages configuration, user controls, and UART traffic while custom Verilog handles the high-throughput ADC interface, buffering, and filtering. We will follow a disciplined flow: write a clear specification, build the Qsys system with IP and custom peripherals, implement and verify RTL in ModelSim, compile in Quartus Prime, then load and exercise the hardware with the JTAG debugger and logic analyzer. Along the way, you will make hardware-software partitioning choices and document testbenches, timing reports, and a demonstration video. By the end you will have a reproducible, graded project with clear deliverables. As you begin, think about which functions must run in hardware for performance and which are easier to manage in software—this is the core engineering trade-off you will practice.

By the end of this capstone you will be able to design a complete FPGA-based embedded system from a specification, integrate custom Verilog peripherals with a NIOS II soft-core inside Qsys, and write embedded C that runs on the processor to manage acquisition and communication. You will follow the FPGA design flow from Qsys assembly through Quartus Prime compilation, verify RTL in ModelSim, and program the hardware for live testing. You will test and debug with JTAG and logic analyzers, and produce a project report that documents block diagrams, RTL testbenches, timing results, and a demonstration video. Each objective maps to a concrete milestone: a working Qsys system, verified Verilog modules, a compiled bitstream, a running NIOS II application, and a recorded demo. These skills are essential because real embedded FPGA projects require coordination of hardware and software, clear verification evidence, and a reproducible delivery for grading or field use. Think about how each objective leads to a deliverable you can show — that clarity will help you plan and execute the project effectively.

This second objectives slide clarifies the practical skills you will show in deliverables. You will demonstrate hardware-software co-design by deciding which functions run as Verilog peripherals and which run in the NIOS II application. You will produce ModelSim testbenches for the ADC interface, circular buffer, and FIR filter, and collect waveforms as verification evidence. You will generate a Quartus Prime compile, inspect resource usage and timing reports, and resolve timing violations with constraint updates. You will use JTAG to load bitstreams, step through C code, and observe signals with a logic analyzer when debugging the ADC path and trigger logic. Finally, you will prepare a clear project report and a short demonstration video showing acquisition, filtering, and UART output. These outputs map directly to the grading rubric and make the engineering choices traceable, which is what evaluators look for when assessing design quality and testing rigor.

Start by writing a concise specification that turns project goals into measurable requirements. For the recommended oscilloscope, specify the ADC channel, sampling resolution, required sample rate up to 1 MSPS, the capture window of 256 samples, buffer sizes, and the trigger mechanism that initiates a capture. Include precise interface definitions: UART baud (115200), button behavior (Button 1 toggles acquisition, Button 2 changes modes), LED status signals, and the NIOS II memories used for code and data. A clear spec avoids late rework: it tells you whether the FIR filter must be implemented in hardware for throughput or if a software routine on NIOS II is sufficient. Include performance constraints such as a 50 MHz system clock and timing margin for the ADC interface. As a concrete example, list the circular buffer as 256 samples in dual-port BRAM and the FIR filter as a 16-tap fixed-coefficient block. A common misconception is that vague goals are acceptable; in practice, missing or fuzzy constraints cause integration delays. Close with a checklist: block diagram, interface table, capture size, trigger conditions, and performance targets — these items become the foundation for Qsys and RTL work.

Qsys is where you assemble the system-level hardware: a NIOS II/f soft-core with its JTAG debug module, program and data memories, UART, timer, GPIO, and the ADC IP. You will add dual-port BRAM for the sample buffer and instantiate custom Avalon peripherals for the ADC interface and FIR filter. Assign base addresses carefully to avoid overlap and document them in your spec so your C code knows where to read and write. A concrete example from the chapter lists 64 KB on-chip memory for program and data, 8 KB of BRAM for the sample buffer, and a UART configured at 115200 baud connected to the USB-UART bridge. A common misconception is that adding IP is enough; in practice you must connect interrupt lines to the NIOS II, provide clocks and resets, and check bus width compatibility. After generating the Qsys system, export the top-level HDL and include the generated system in your top-level Verilog. Finish this step with a short sanity test: compile the board support package and run a trivial UART echo to confirm the communication path is functional. This early integration check saves time later when you add custom peripherals.

Two custom Verilog modules are central to reliable acquisition: the adc_interface and the circular_buffer. The adc_interface reads the ADC IP core, detects valid samples, and presents a clean data-valid handshake to downstream logic. Define explicit signals: data_out, data_valid, write_enable, and a sampled timestamp or sample counter if needed. The circular_buffer implements 256-sample storage in dual-port BRAM. Use separate read and write pointers with modulo arithmetic for wrap-around and ensure that the write pointer advances only when data_valid is asserted. For dual-port BRAM, one port services writes from adc_interface while the other serves reads from NIOS II or the FIR filter. A concrete implementation detail: implement full/empty detection by tracking a sample count or comparing read and write pointers carefully. A common mistake is failing to handle concurrent read/write and reading stale data; mitigate this by using proper synchronizers when crossing clock domains or by using single-clock semantics if all logic shares the same clock. Close by writing a ModelSim testbench that drives ADC sample patterns and verifies buffer wrap-around and read-after-write correctness. Design adc_interface and circular_buffer means use dual-port bram with independent read/write pointers, clear data-valid handshake, and test wrap-around with a modelsim testbench.. In practical terms, signals, data-valid handshakes, dual-port bram access, and wrap-around logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A 16-tap FIR filter is a common choice for low-pass filtering of ADC samples. In hardware, implement it as a multiply-accumulate engine that reads a sample stream, multiplies by fixed coefficients, and accumulates results. Fixed coefficients let you use constant multipliers and possibly resource-saving optimizations. Pipeline the multiply-accumulate path to achieve higher throughput: break the operations into stages so each pipeline stage has less combinational delay, which raises the maximum clock frequency. The chapter recommends a hardware FIR to demonstrate hardware-software partitioning; use Avalon slave interfaces to feed samples from the circular buffer into the FIR peripheral and provide a ready/valid handshake for the filtered output. A concrete example: when the FIR is hardware-accelerated, the NIOS II can trigger the filter over a block of 256 samples and read filtered outputs at leisure over the bus. A common misconception is that more taps are always better; in practice, more taps increase latency and resource use. Close with a verification step: simulate the FIR input of a sine plus noise and confirm the expected attenuation or frequency response in ModelSim waveforms.

The NIOS II software orchestrates acquisition and user interaction. Start by initializing UART, ADC, timer, and GPIO. The main loop waits for a button press, starts ADC acquisition, collects 256 samples into memory or triggers the FIR filter, reads back filtered values, and sends them to the PC via UART. Implement a timer ISR to blink a status LED periodically so you know the system is alive. Include a UART command handler to change filter modes or trigger thresholds from the PC. The chapter includes a concrete temperature-monitoring C example that demonstrates reading the ADC, checking a button, and printing results periodically; use that structure for the oscilloscope code. A common mistake in embedded code is polling without debouncing buttons or without considering ISR preemption; prefer edge detection for button presses and keep ISR code short. After writing the application, test it first on the instruction set simulator, then on hardware with JTAG debug. The final step is to send captured data as ASCII numbers or a simple ASCII waveform so the instructor can verify functionality from the terminal output.
